plot_extraction.response_text:
A jovial German baron grows bored with hunting and revelry, so he marries the daughter of a neighboring nobleman. His domineering wife gradually forces him to dismiss his companions and abandon everything he enjoys. Burdened by twelve children, an interfering mother-in-law, mounting debts, and the prospect of a thirteenth child, he decides to kill himself.

Before doing so, he retreats with wine and a pipe to a private room, where he encounters the grotesque Genius of Despair and Suicide. Their conversation inadvertently exposes the absurdity of suicide: people kill themselves from both poverty and wealth, present troubles may yet be remedied, and death offers no guarantee of improvement. Recovering his humor and resolve, the baron rejects suicide, frightening the apparition away with laughter.

He then confronts his wife and in-laws, returns to hunting, and lives for many more years as a happy, though not wealthy, man while raising his large family.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts a comic Gothic style, combining the apparatus of a medieval German romance—an ancient castle, ancestral violence, hunting parties, melancholy, supernatural visitations and contemplated suicide—with a persistently irreverent, satirical treatment. Its Gothic scenery is deliberately conventional and exaggerated: moonlit galleries, howling forests, gloomy chambers and a corpse-like apparition are introduced only to be undercut by practical explanations, bathos or absurd detail. The ancestor’s murder, for example, is treated as a financial and administrative matter, while his chapel becomes an “apology” and a “receipt from Heaven.” Horror is therefore less an end in itself than a framework for farce, social criticism and moral comedy.

The narrator is conspicuous, conversational and knowingly intrusive. He addresses the reader indirectly, admits uncertainty, digresses into personal opinions and repeatedly interrupts the tale with mock explanations. Remarks such as “I needn’t say,” “I contend that this is not fair” and “I have no means of knowing” create the manner of an anecdote told aloud by an amused, opinionated raconteur. This voice claims limited knowledge while exercising complete comic control, using feigned innocence to expose the absurdity of aristocratic customs, pedigree, marriage, politics and sentimental convention. General reflections often grow out of verbal associations rather than strict narrative necessity, giving the prose an improvisatory, club-story quality.

The dominant tone is genial but sharp-edged irony. Nobility is mocked through inflated titles, ridiculous names and mechanical hierarchies: the baron’s followers are reduced to “four-and-twenty Lincoln greens,” distinguished from their master chiefly by coarser cloth and thicker soles. Violence, drunkenness and domestic tyranny are narrated with jaunty understatement. The baron inserts a knife into a traveller, threatens to cut off a rival’s nose and kicks his retainers as though these were minor breaches of etiquette. Conversely, supposedly elevated emotions are translated into physical or comic actions: a father “shed a wink of joy,” filial sacrifice prevents a castle from being thrown out of a window, and solemn pledges are measured in quantities of wine. This recurring mismatch between subject and treatment produces the story’s characteristic burlesque.

The diction alternates between mock-heroic formality and lively colloquial speech. Elevated phrases such as “venerable building,” “dangerous distinction,” “appalling significance” and “ere the sun goes down” coexist with “queer customer,” “look sharp,” “a good one” and “put a good face on the matter.” Archaic or romance-inflected vocabulary establishes the period atmosphere, while colloquialisms puncture it. Comic specificity is important: moustachios, russet boots, imperial pints, coffin handles, a sharpened hunting knife and a nursery window barred against the moat all make the fantasy tangible while preserving its caricatural quality. Invented Germanic names such as Koldwethout, Grogzwig and Swillenhausen contribute sound-based humour and signal that the setting is an English comic fantasy of Germany rather than realistic cultural representation.

Sentences are often long, cumulative and parenthetical, driven by semicolons, qualifications and escalating lists. The narrator likes to begin with a simple proposition and then extend it through comic logic until it reaches an absurd conclusion, as in the meditation on why later-born people must possess longer pedigrees. Repetition supplies both rhythm and exaggeration: “little by little, and bit by bit, and day by day, and year by year” charts the baron’s domestic defeat, while repeated numerical formulas turn people and actions into comic inventory. Parallel constructions, reversals and antitheses are frequent, especially formulations that correct or intensify themselves, such as the “pleasures of the table, or the pleasures of under the table.” The prose also favours accumulations of near-synonyms—“jolly, roystering, rollicking, merry-making”—whose abundance enacts the excess being described.

Dialogue is brisk, theatrical and built around repetition, literal-mindedness and reversal. Exchanges frequently resemble comic duels, with one speaker’s wording immediately seized and returned by the other. The supernatural conversation is especially laconic: the baron’s blunt questions and the apparition’s dry answers strip the scene of conventional terror. The Genius of Despair and Suicide is rendered simultaneously grotesque and bureaucratic, complaining of a busy schedule and treating self-destruction as a professional transaction. His increasing impatience contrasts with the baron’s growing curiosity, so that the intended victim gradually takes control of the interview. Dialogue also individualises through tempo rather than subtle psychology: the baron is forceful and practical, the baroness manipulative through soft imperatives and swooning, and the genius petulant, evasive and allergic to laughter.

The narrative structure is episodic and strongly shaped by escalation. It begins with a broad comic portrait of the baron’s bachelor life, introduces marriage as an attempted cure for boredom, then converts that marriage into a sequence of accumulating restrictions, children, interfering relations and financial trouble. These pressures lead to the apparent crisis of suicide. The supernatural visitation then reverses the downward movement: every objection offered by the genius prompts the baron to imagine a remedy, and every attempt to deepen despair produces hope. The climax is not an act of violence but laughter, which physically repels the allegorical embodiment of despair. A compact retrospective ending confirms the baron’s reform and supplies an explicit moral.

Characterisation is deliberately broad and caricatural. The baron is defined by appetite, physicality, impulsiveness and resilience rather than introspection. His retainers operate as a comic chorus, pale faces and permanently coloured noses responding in unison. The women are presented through a period domestic satire in which marriage becomes a contest for authority; the narrator’s remarks about wives and Members of Parliament extend the private joke into social commentary. The characterisation relies on stereotypes and comic types, but the baron’s recovery gives him a simple emotional arc from heedless pleasure, through subjection and despair, to purposeful self-command.

The supernatural figure functions as an embodied abstraction, linking the tale to allegory and moral fable. His costume literalises death through coffin furniture, pall cloth and the stake through his body, yet these macabre details are handled with visual extravagance and deadpan comedy. The apparition’s weakness before moderation, hope and laughter makes the moral mechanism transparent: despair survives by encouraging one-sided thought, while comic perspective restores proportion. The final advice states this philosophy openly, recommending that sufferers examine “both sides of the question” and magnify the better one. Although drinking and smoking are playfully offered as remedies, the deeper prescription is action, perspective and refusal to brood.

Overall, the style is exuberant, digressive, performative and anti-solemn. It repeatedly erects the expectations of romance, tragedy or terror and collapses them into common sense, wordplay and comic materialism. Its principal techniques are mock-heroic inflation, bathos, hyperbole, numerical repetition, intrusive narration, grotesque visual detail, rhythmic listing and rapid repartee. Even its moralising remains playful: the tale advocates optimism not through earnest sermonising, but by making despair look pompous, uncomfortable and ridiculous. ## THE BARON OF DONNERDUST

In the oldest and draughtiest quarter of Germany—where the mountains are peaked like nightcaps, the fir trees grow for the express purpose of howling after sunset, and every castle has at least one tower which no prudent person enters without a lantern and a written explanation of his business—there stood, some centuries ago, the venerable fortress of Donderdust.

It had seven courts, nine turrets, eleven chimneys, and a moat so green that the frogs were ashamed of it. Over the principal gate hung the stone likeness of Baron Wolfbold von Donderdust, who had founded the family by killing his elder brother, marrying his brother’s widow, and purchasing the approval of the Church at a very reasonable rate. He afterwards built a chapel to show his penitence; and as the chapel cost almost exactly what he had obtained by the murder, it was commonly regarded as an apology in stone and a receipt from Heaven.

His descendant, Baron Hildebrand von Donderdust, was a broad, red-faced, round-bodied gentleman, with black moustachios, russet boots, a green hunting coat, and a laugh which shook birds from the roof. He possessed a good estate, a bad cellar—for no cellar is good which is often empty—and five-and-twenty followers, including four-and-twenty men in Lincoln green and one steward in brown, who was much more dangerous than all the rest because he understood arithmetic.

The green men hunted with the baron, drank with the baron, sang with the baron, quarrelled with the baron, and fell under the table with the baron. They were distinguished from him chiefly by having coarser coats, thicker heads, thinner purses, and no legal claim to the castle. Their noses were of various shapes but one colour; and when ranged along the lower table after supper, with tankards before them and boar-spears behind, they presented as noble a picture of feudal attachment as any man could wish to see—provided he did not wish to smell it.

The baron was then thirty-five, though several village maidens asserted that he was younger, and several village fathers that he ought to have known better. He had never been ill except after drinking, never melancholy except before dinner, and never frightened except by a bill. He rose at daybreak, hunted till sunset, supped till midnight, and spent the remaining hours in such innocent recreations as throwing knives at the door, singing war-songs in the chapel, and waking the steward to inquire how much money was left.

“None, my lord,” the steward generally replied.

“Then we know where it is,” said the baron. “Bring wine.”

This was a satisfactory arrangement while it lasted. But even pleasure, when repeated every day, becomes as tiresome as virtue; and one winter, after hunting the same wolves through the same forest, missing the same stag by the same oak tree, and hearing his companions sing the same thirty-seven verses about the Maiden of the Rhine, Baron Hildebrand became bored.

Boredom is a dangerous distinction in a great man. A poor man who is bored may mend his shoes, dig his garden, or quarrel with his landlord; but a nobleman has nothing between boredom and matrimony except politics, and politics had not yet been invented in that neighbourhood.

“I must have a change,” said the baron.

The four-and-twenty green men stopped drinking and looked pale, which, in their case, meant pale everywhere but the nose.

“A change of wine?” asked Klaus, the captain.

“No.”

“Of horses?”

“No.”

“Of steward?”

The steward coughed.

“No. I shall marry.”

At this appalling word the company groaned, and one old retainer slipped beneath the table from pure feudal sensibility.

The lady selected was Fraulein Adelgunda von Schnappenschloss, only daughter of the neighbouring Count of that name. She was tall, fair, blue-eyed, soft-spoken, and accomplished in embroidery, fainting, and obtaining her own way. Her father was celebrated for having fought three duels without injuring anybody, which showed either unusual humanity or very bad aim. Her mother, the Countess Ermengarda, was a woman of majestic proportions and unanswerable opinions. She had directed her husband for thirty years and had brought him, by patience, tears, reproaches, headaches, and locked cupboards, into a state of perfect domestic happiness.

Baron Hildebrand rode to Schnappenschloss with all his followers, thirty hounds, two falcons, three casks of wine, and a sharpened hunting knife. The last was not intended as a present; but a gentleman in those days never knew whom he might meet on the road, and many excellent friendships began with an attempt to cut off somebody’s nose.

The Count received him with open arms, chiefly because the baron had brought the wine. Adelgunda lowered her eyes. The Countess raised hers. The twenty-four green men emptied their cups. Before the third cask had been broached, the marriage was settled.

“My daughter is a tender flower,” said the Countess.

“I’ll take care nobody treads on her,” said Hildebrand.

“She has delicate nerves.”

“Our walls are thick.”

“She cannot bear noise.”

The green men, who were roaring a chorus in the courtyard, broke a bench at that moment.

“They can sing outside,” said the baron.

“She dislikes bloodshed.”

“I never shed blood indoors if I can help it.”

“She must not be contradicted.”

“Certainly not,” said Hildebrand, who had heard only half the sentence and understood none of it.

Adelgunda smiled. The Count shed a wink of joy into his cup. The Countess embraced the baron as a son whom she intended to improve; and the marriage took place with such magnificence that six neighbouring families were ruined by trying to imitate it.

For the first month, Baron Hildebrand declared matrimony the finest sport in Christendom. Adelgunda called him her lion, her eagle, her thunderbolt, and her sweet little Hildebrand. She admired his moustachios, praised his horses, and listened to the first three verses of the Maiden of the Rhine with every appearance of consciousness. He presented her with jewels, falcons, silk gowns, and the key to the household stores.

The last gift was the most important. A woman may mislay jewels, neglect falcons, and tire of silk, but she seldom forgets a key.

Little by little, and bit by bit, and day by day, the castle altered. The hunting horns were removed from the great hall because their appearance encouraged noise. The boar-spears were carried to the armoury because their points offended Adelgunda’s nerves. The hounds were sent from the courtyard to the outer kennels, from the outer kennels to the village, and from the village to a cousin of the Countess, who had no use for them but liked acquiring property.

Then came the turn of the four-and-twenty green men.

“My love,” said the baroness one morning, “that red-nosed fellow Klaus stared at me.”

“Klaus stares at everything,” said Hildebrand. “His eyes were made so.”

“I tremble whenever I see him.”

“Then don’t see him.”

“How can I help seeing him when he is here?”

The baron considered this. It was an unfortunate habit of his to consider the last question put to him and forget all that had gone before.

“Klaus!” he cried. “Take six men and hunt on the northern estate.”

Adelgunda kissed him; and within a fortnight she trembled at seven others.

Some were discharged because they sang, some because they snored, some because they wore muddy boots, and one because he had laughed while the baroness’s lapdog was being sick. The last offence I contend was not fairly proved; for the man declared that he had laughed at the dog before it was sick and become serious immediately afterwards. But justice, especially domestic justice, is less concerned with time than with example.

At length only old Dietrich remained. He had carried Hildebrand when an infant, saved him from drowning when a boy, followed him in three border fights, and once allowed himself to be bitten by a wolf rather than wake the baron before noon.

“My angel,” said Adelgunda, “Dietrich frightens the children.”

At that time there were four children.

“He loves them,” said Hildebrand.

“He gives them knives.”

“Small knives.”

“He teaches them to swear.”

“Only at wolves.”

“He says your mother was the finest woman in Germany.”

“So she was.”

Adelgunda burst into tears.

Dietrich went that evening.

Children, meanwhile, arrived with a punctuality worthy of better-regulated persons. There was a son the first year, twin daughters the second, another son the third, three daughters in two years, and so on, until twelve young Donderdusts inhabited the castle, shouted in the passages, tumbled down the stairs, pulled the tapestry from the walls, and attempted to sail across the moat in a cradle. Iron bars were placed across the nursery windows, not, as visitors supposed, to keep robbers out, but to keep the family in.

The Countess Ermengarda now came to assist her daughter. She brought six trunks, two parrots, a physician, a lapdog, and the intention of remaining for a week. At the end of eight years she was still there.

Her husband came also, because he had grown accustomed to being directed and felt lonely without it. He occupied a chamber over the kitchen, played cards with the chaplain, and never interfered except when ordered by the Countess, at which times he interfered with great spirit.

The expenses of Donderdust increased. There were nurses, tutors, physicians, dancing masters, fencing masters, tailors, pastry cooks, French dolls, Italian singers, Dutch toys, and German bills. The baron sold two farms, then four vineyards, then the silver drinking cups, after which the Countess observed that the family was living beyond its means.

“My means lived very comfortably before your family came,” said Hildebrand.

“My family!” cried Adelgunda.

“My family!” thundered the Countess.

“My family?” repeated the Count, looking up from his cards.

That night the baron slept in the west tower.

He had long ago ceased to hunt. His green coat grew tight in the shoulders and loose at the courage. His moustachios drooped. He walked softly past the drawing room, ate whatever was left after the children, and drank weak wine on the physician’s assurance that strong wine encouraged independent thought. If he laughed, the baroness had a headache; if he sang, the baby woke; if he proposed riding, rain was expected; and if there was no rain, one of the children was indisposed, which came to much the same thing, except that the child generally recovered before the weather.

One November evening the steward entered with a packet of accounts. He laid them upon the table in the manner of a physician placing his hand upon a corpse.

“How bad?” asked the baron.

“Very bad, my lord.”

“Can we pay?”

“No, my lord.”

“Can we borrow?”

“We have.”

“Can we sell?”

“We have.”

“What remains?”

“The castle, the forest, the northern meadows, and your title.”

“What is the title worth?”

“Nothing, my lord.”

“Thank Heaven,” said Hildebrand. “We can keep that.”

At this moment Adelgunda came in, pale and interesting, followed by the Countess, pale and commanding.

“My dear Hildebrand,” said the baroness, “I have news.”

The baron looked at the twelve family portraits recently painted upon the opposite wall. The youngest sitter had swallowed a brush during the final session, and the bill included it.

“No,” said Hildebrand.

“Yes,” murmured Adelgunda.

“A thirteenth blessing,” said the Countess.

The baron stared at the accounts, at his wife, at his mother-in-law, and lastly at the ancestral sword hanging above the fireplace. Baron Wolfbold had used that sword upon his brother, three creditors, and a tax collector. Hildebrand’s thoughts took a gloomy turn.

He bowed, left the room, and walked along the moonlit gallery. The wind moaned among the turrets; shutters banged; a raven flapped against the windows; and something white glided across the end of the passage. It was only a nurse in a nightcap carrying a basin, but at such a time even a basin may possess appalling significance.

The baron entered an abandoned chamber in the oldest tower. No one used it because an ancestor was said to have murdered a traveller there and hidden the body beneath the floor. The traveller had subsequently been found alive in Prague, but the room retained its reputation, reputations being far easier to acquire than to correct.

Hildebrand locked the door. He placed a pistol on the table, a knife beside it, a rope beside the knife, and a cup of poison beside the rope. He had brought all four because he had not decided which method was most becoming to his rank. Then he produced a flagon of old wine and a pipe.

“A man should not die thirsty,” he said, “nor in a hurry.”

He filled his cup, lit his pipe, and stretched his boots toward the fire. The wine was excellent. The tobacco was better. After the second cup the pistol looked less persuasive; after the third, the rope appeared positively foolish. Nevertheless, he had formed a resolution and was preparing to remember it when a cold hand touched his shoulder.

The baron turned.

Beside him stood a figure as tall as a coffin set upright and much less cheerful. Its face was yellow, its eyes green, its cheeks hollow, and its mouth drawn down at the corners as if it had been fed on vinegar from infancy. It wore a cloak of black pall cloth, fastened with coffin handles; a wreath of faded cypress encircled its head; and through the middle of its body projected a wooden stake, which must have made sitting inconvenient. Small silver skulls decorated its shoes. One lace was undone.

“Who the devil are you?” asked Hildebrand.

“Not the devil,” replied the figure. “He has better quarters.”

“Then take your hand off my shoulder.”

The figure did so, though with an offended air.

“I am the Genius of Despair and Suicide.”

“A busy profession?”

“Extremely. I have seven appointments before dawn. You are the third.”

“Who were the others?”

“A wealthy prince who has eaten too much supper, and a beggar who has eaten none.”

Hildebrand puffed his pipe.

“Do both kill themselves for the same reason?”

“Certainly not.”

“What is the prince’s reason?”

“He has everything and is tired of it.”

“And the beggar’s?”

“He has nothing and is tired of that.”

The baron considered.

“It seems difficult to satisfy people.”

“It is impossible,” said the Genius, with professional pride.

“And you have come to assist me?”

“To hurry you. I cannot spend the whole night in one castle. Choose your instrument.”

Hildebrand looked at the pistol.

“Will it hurt?”

“For a moment.”

“And afterwards?”

“I cannot say.”

“You are the Genius of Suicide and don’t know what comes afterwards?”

“My department ends at the act.”

“Bad administration,” said the baron. “If my steward conducted business in that fashion, I should dismiss him.”

“Your affairs are ruined,” replied the Genius. “Your pleasures are gone. Your companions are scattered. Your wife rules you, your mother-in-law insults you, your creditors surround you, and your thirteenth child is approaching with all reasonable speed. What remains?”

“Nothing,” said Hildebrand gloomily.

“Precisely. Shoot yourself.”

The baron lifted the pistol, then put it down.

“Wait. My affairs are ruined, you say?”

“Hopelessly.”

“Could I reduce expenses?”

“You might.”

“Sell the southern timber?”

“Possibly.”

“Dismiss the Italian singer, the French tutor, the physician, the dancing master, the pastry cook, the Countess’s two parrots, and the lapdog?”

“You could.”

“Then my affairs are not hopeless.”

“They are unpleasant.”

“Unpleasant is not hopeless. This wine is unpleasant when empty, but I fill the cup.”

He did so.

The Genius shifted his stake impatiently.

“Your old life is destroyed.”

“I might begin another.”

“At your age?”

“I am forty-seven.”

“Exactly.”

“My grandfather hunted wolves at eighty.”

“He was killed by one.”

“Yes, but he enjoyed the hunt.”

The Genius tapped one skull-tipped shoe upon the floor.

“Your friends have deserted you.”

“I dismissed them.”

“Then they will hate you.”

“They are Germans,” said Hildebrand. “They will forgive me if I provide supper.”

“Your wife will forbid it.”

“Ah,” said the baron.

He smoked for a little while, and the Genius smiled a corpse-like smile.

“There!” said the apparition. “You see. You are mastered.”

“I have permitted myself to be mastered.”

“The distinction is trifling.”

“It may be, but it is mine. If a man puts his own head under a pump, he should not accuse the pump of tyranny. I shall take it out.”

“Your wife will weep.”

“She always does.”

“She will faint.”

“I shall place a cushion behind her.”

“Her mother will denounce you.”

“I shall provide a carriage.”

“Her father will challenge you.”

“I shall let him aim first.”

This answer plainly distressed the Genius.

“Think of your children,” he said hastily. “Twelve already, and another coming. They will consume your fortune, disturb your peace, and divide your estate.”

“They may also grow up.”

“They may.”

“They may help me.”

“They may not.”

“One may become a soldier.”

“And be killed.”

“One a priest.”

“And become fat.”

“One a merchant.”

“And cheat you.”

“One may remain at home.”

“And annoy you.”

“Then,” cried Hildebrand, “they have every prospect of becoming ordinary useful members of society. I see no reason to shoot myself on their account.”

“You were eager enough when I arrived.”

“I had not examined the matter.”

“Examination is fatal to my business,” muttered the Genius.

“What was that?”

“Nothing. Take the poison. It is quiet.”

“Does it taste bad?”

“Very.”

“Then I object on principle. I have swallowed bad wine to please my father-in-law, bad medicine to please the physician, and bad advice to please my wife. I will not swallow bad poison to please you.”

The Genius’s green eyes flashed.

“You are miserable!”

“At present.”

“You have been miserable for years!”

“Quite true.”

“You will be miserable tomorrow!”

“I have no means of knowing. I have not tried tomorrow.”

“Your debts—”

“May be arranged.”

“Your household—”

“May be reduced.”

“Your wife—”

“May be reasoned with.”

The Genius gave a dry, rattling chuckle.

“That is the wildest hope yet.”

“Then she may be reasoned without.”

“You make light of everything.”

“No,” said Hildebrand, filling another cup. “I have made everything heavy. That was the trouble.”

He rose. The black figure appeared less tall now, though this may have been because the baron had straightened his back.

“Sit down!” cried the Genius.

“I have sat down for twelve years.”

“Despair!”

“I have tried it.”

“Die!”

“Not tonight.”

“You made an appointment.”

“I made no appointment with you.”

“You laid out the instruments.”

“I was comparing them.”

“You cannot dismiss me!”

“My wife dismissed Klaus, Dietrich, four-and-twenty hunters, thirty hounds, and a falcon that had been in the family longer than she had. I have learned something from her.”

The Genius advanced, his cloak rustling like dead leaves in a churchyard.

“Beware! If you live, there will be quarrels, toil, humiliation, poverty, screaming children, unpaid bills, grey hairs, rheumatism, and perhaps gout.”

“Very likely.”

“There will be disappointment.”

“Certainly.”

“Trouble.”

“No doubt.”

“Death at the end.”

“Of course.”

“Then why laugh?”

“Because,” said Baron Hildebrand, beginning with a chuckle in his waistcoat and ending with a roar among the rafters, “you offer me death as a cure for death!”

He laughed until the cups danced, the pistol rolled from the table, and dust fell out of the ancestral curtains. He laughed at the coffin handles, at the cypress wreath, at the silver skulls, at the wooden stake, and especially at the undone shoestring. The more he laughed, the smaller the Genius became. His pall-cloth cloak shrank to a widow’s handkerchief; his stake dwindled to a splinter; his green eyes faded like bad lamps at sunrise.

“Stop!” squeaked the apparition. “This is indecent!”

The baron laughed louder.

The Genius folded inward like a scorched parchment, slipped through a crack beside the hearth, and vanished with a smell of damp ashes and disappointed vinegar.

At breakfast, Baron Hildebrand appeared in his old green coat, which burst at one button but otherwise behaved nobly. His moustachios stood out. A hunting horn hung at his side.

“My dear,” said Adelgunda, “what does this mean?”

“It means breakfast first and business afterwards.”

The Countess drew herself up.

“I demand—”

“A carriage will be ready for you at noon.”

She sat down very suddenly.

The Count rose. “Sir, I shall not permit—”

“Your carriage will be the same one. It is economical.”

Adelgunda began to weep. The baron placed a cushion behind her.

“The singer, tutors, physician, dancing master, pastry cook, parrots, and dog leave today,” he continued. “The children will keep one tutor, two nurses, and all their limbs if possible. The steward will settle with the creditors. I shall sell the southern timber and hunt the northern forest. Klaus and the others are coming to supper.”

“You monster!” cried the Countess.

“Madam,” replied Hildebrand, “I have been called worse by a gentleman in coffin handles.”

He kissed his wife, rang for breakfast, and blew the hunting horn out of the window. The blast rolled over the moat and through the forest. Before noon, men in faded green were hurrying toward Donderdust from every road, with red noses, muddy boots, cracked horns, and forgiveness enough for any offence that included supper.

The baroness did not yield at once. I needn’t say that; no sensible person ever expected she would. There were tears, faintings, locked doors, messages through servants, appeals to the children, and one alarming threat to return to her mother, which lost much of its force because her mother had already returned to her. But Hildebrand remained cheerful, affectionate, and immovable; and firmness, when it is not accompanied by shouting, is a very puzzling weapon.

In time Adelgunda discovered that she preferred a husband who laughed to one who crept, that children could survive plain cakes, and that a castle containing hunters was no noisier than a castle containing twelve young Donderdusts. She even permitted the hounds to return, though not to the drawing room.

The thirteenth child arrived safely and proved to be a daughter, who later married a banker and restored half the family fortune—a fact which the Genius of Despair had neglected to predict, his department, as he observed, being badly administered.

Baron Hildebrand lived to eighty-two. He never became rich, but he paid his debts, educated his children, hunted moderately, drank with discrimination, and laughed without permission. When trouble came, as trouble will come even to castles with seven courts and nine turrets, he looked at both sides of it, and if one side appeared black, he polished the other until it shone.

This is not a grand remedy, perhaps; but it frightened away a Genius, preserved a baron, raised thirteen children, and kept the castle of Donderdust from falling into the hands of the creditors—which is as much as can reasonably be expected from any philosophy.

# The Keeper of Lost Hours

Every morning at precisely seven, Elias Vale unlocked the brass door beneath the western clock tower and listened to the city wake.

First came the bakery carts, their iron wheels rattling over the stones. Then the river ferries sounded their low horns in the fog. Windows opened. Dogs barked. Somewhere, almost always, a child cried because the day had arrived too soon.

Above it all, the city clocks began to strike.

They did not strike together. They never had. The clock at the courthouse was three seconds slow, the station clock seven seconds fast, and the green clock above Saint Orra’s Hospital sometimes forgot an entire minute. Yet the people of Bellwether trusted them. They glanced upward before appointments, counted their chimes during sleepless nights, and set their lives by those great black hands.

Only Elias knew that the clocks did more than measure time.

They collected what people lost.

Beneath the western tower lay the Archive of Mislaid Hours, a long underground hall filled with shelves, cabinets, and thousands of glass bottles. Each bottle held a fragment of time that had slipped away unnoticed: five minutes wasted waiting for rain to stop, an afternoon forgotten after a fever, the final second before an accident, a summer blurred by grief.

The bottles shone softly in the dark. Some contained golden light. Others swirled with grey mist. A few were black and cold, and Elias kept those locked behind iron mesh.

He had been Keeper of the Archive for thirty-eight years.

His duties were simple. Every night, hidden pipes carried lost time from the clocks into a copper receiving tank. Every morning, Elias separated the hours, labeled them, and placed them on the shelves.

He never opened a bottle.

That was the first rule.

The second rule was never to return lost time to the person who had lost it.

The third was never to ask why.

Elias had obeyed all three rules until the morning he found the blue hour.

It waited at the bottom of the receiving tank, shining like moonlight beneath deep water. He lifted it carefully with silver tongs and placed it on his worktable.

The bottle was small, no larger than his thumb. Blue light turned slowly inside it, carrying tiny shapes that vanished whenever he tried to focus on them. A hand. A ribbon. A woman’s face.

Elias stopped breathing.

Around the neck of the bottle was a paper label.

ELIAS VALE  
14 OCTOBER  
5:16 P.M. TO 6:16 P.M.  
FORTY YEARS OVERDUE

He read it three times.

The Archive was silent except for the ticking of the regulator clock on the wall.

Elias looked toward the tall ledger resting on its oak stand. Each recovered hour had to be recorded there. He opened the book and ran a finger down the date.

There it was.

14 October, forty years before.

Entry number 718,442.

One hour.

Owner: Elias Vale.

Status: Unrecovered.

He had no memory of losing an hour that day. In fact, he remembered the date clearly. It was the day before his wedding.

He had been twenty-three. Impatient. Nervous. Certain that his life was about to begin. He remembered buying white roses for Clara. He remembered dropping one in the street and watching a carriage wheel crush it into the mud. He remembered arriving late at her father’s house.

And he remembered Clara standing in the doorway, pale and trembling, saying, “I can’t marry you.”

The wedding never happened.

Clara left Bellwether the following morning. Some said she went north. Others said she crossed the sea. Elias never learned the truth. He wrote letters that came back unopened, then letters that never came back at all.

Years passed.

He became the Keeper. Clara became a silence he carried from room to room.

Yet now, on his table, was an hour from the last evening they had spent in the same city.

The regulator clock ticked.

Elias reached for the bottle.

His fingers closed around the cool glass.

Then the brass door above the stairs opened.

“Mr. Vale?”

Elias released the bottle and covered it with a cloth.

Footsteps descended.

A girl appeared at the end of the aisle, wearing a yellow coat and carrying a wicker basket. She was about twelve, with dark hair cut unevenly below her ears.

“The sign says no visitors,” Elias said.

“The sign outside says Clock Repairs.”

“The other sign.”

“I didn’t see another sign.”

“Then it is badly placed.”

The girl came closer. “My mother says the western clock stole something.”

Elias frowned. “Clocks don’t steal.”

“My mother says they do.”

“Your mother is mistaken.”

“She usually is,” the girl said, “but not about this.”

She set her basket on the worktable. Inside lay a broken pocket watch, a loaf of bread, and a white pigeon with one black eye.

The pigeon blinked at Elias.

“What is all this?”

“Lunch,” the girl said, pointing to the bread. “A patient,” she added, indicating the bird. “And evidence.”

She picked up the watch.

“My father carried this. It stopped the night he disappeared.”

Elias examined it. The silver case was scratched, and the crystal had cracked across the center. The hands pointed to eleven minutes past nine.

“When did he disappear?”

“Last winter. During the Long Fog.”

Elias remembered it. For nine nights, a fog had risen from the river and swallowed the streets. People lost their way between neighboring houses. The clocks sounded strange and distant. By the time the fog cleared, seven citizens had vanished.

“Go to the constables,” Elias said.

“We did.”

“And?”

“They said my father probably ran away.”

“Did he?”

“No.”

“You sound certain.”

“He left his good boots.”

Elias looked at her.

The girl folded her arms. “Nobody runs away in winter wearing slippers.”

It was a reasonable argument.

“What is your name?”

“Mara Venn.”

Elias searched his memory. “Your father repaired the northern bridge.”

“He designed it.”

“It leans.”

“Only in strong winds.”

The pigeon escaped the basket and fluttered onto a shelf. Its wings disturbed three bottles, setting them chiming against one another.

“Get that creature out of here!”

Mara caught the bird and tucked it under her arm.

In the confusion, the cloth slid from the blue bottle.

Mara stared.

“That one has your name on it.”

Elias covered it again.

“You can read upside down?”

“My father taught me.”

“A dangerous habit.”

“What’s inside?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing doesn’t glow.”

Elias pointed toward the stairs. “Leave.”

Mara lifted her basket. At the first step, she stopped.

“My father used to say that when a grown man tells a child to leave, it’s usually because the child has asked the right question.”

“Your father sounds exhausting.”

“He is. Was. Is.”

Her face changed on the final word, the certainty cracking just enough for Elias to glimpse the fear beneath it.

Then she climbed the stairs and was gone.

Elias stood alone again.

The blue light pulsed under the cloth.

He spent the morning pretending not to notice it. He sorted a quarter-hour lost by a violinist during a performance. He bottled twelve minutes from a woman who had stared at an empty chair. He catalogued three seconds belonging to a condemned prisoner.

At noon, he carried the blue bottle to the iron furnace at the rear of the Archive.

Lost hours were never destroyed. That was another rule, although no one called it the fourth. The furnace existed for damaged bottles and corrupted fragments, not time itself.

Elias opened the furnace door.

Heat struck his face.

He imagined dropping the bottle into the flames. The glass would melt. The hour would escape, perhaps vanishing forever, perhaps sinking into the stones. He would never know what it contained.

He almost did it.

Then a voice whispered from inside the bottle.

“Elias.”

Clara’s voice.

His hand jerked. The bottle slipped.

He caught it against his chest.

For several moments, he stood before the open furnace, trembling.

Then every clock in Bellwether struck noon.

The sound rolled through the city, through the tower, and down into the Archive. Thousands of bottles answered with faint, bright chimes.

Among them, from a shelf near the ceiling, came a dull silver note.

Elias looked up.

The shelf held time recovered during the Long Fog.

He fetched a ladder and climbed. Nine grey bottles stood in a row, one for each night. Eight were sealed.

The ninth had cracked.

A thread of mist leaked from its side.

Elias carried it to the table and checked its label.

NIGHT OF 22 JANUARY  
COLLECTIVE LOSS  
9:11 P.M. TO 9:12 P.M.  
SOURCE: NORTHERN CLOCK

One minute. Lost by the entire city.

The same minute in which Mara’s father’s watch had stopped.

Elias felt the old rules gathering around him like stern ghosts.

Do not open.

Do not return.

Do not ask.

He placed the grey bottle beside the blue one.

Then he went upstairs, locked the brass door, and crossed the city to find Mara Venn.

She lived with her mother above a candle shop on River Street. Bells chimed as Elias entered. The air smelled of wax, cinnamon, and smoke.

Mara sat behind the counter, feeding crumbs to the pigeon.

“I knew you’d come,” she said.

“No, you didn’t.”

“I was fairly sure.”

“Where is your mother?”

“Delivering mourning candles.”

“Do people need special candles for mourning?”

“They cost more if we call them special.”

Elias set the grey bottle on the counter.

Mara’s expression sharpened.

“This was collected the night your father vanished. It contains one minute lost by everyone in Bellwether.”

“Open it.”

“No.”

“Then why did you bring it?”

“A moment of weakness.”

“Have another.”

“Mara, lost time is dangerous. People think they want the past returned, but they rarely understand what that means.”

“I don’t want the past. I want my father.”

“You may find only a memory.”

“That’s more than the constables found.”

Elias looked through the shop window. The afternoon sun flashed on the river. Across the street, two boys chased each other between carts, spending seconds they believed would never run out.

“Bring the watch,” he said.

They returned to the tower before dusk.

In the Archive, Elias placed the broken watch inside a chalk circle. Around it, he arranged twelve mirrors, one for each number on a clock face. The grey bottle stood at the center.

“What will happen?” Mara asked.

“I don’t know.”

“That’s not comforting.”

“It wasn’t intended to be.”

He gave her dark goggles and put on his own.

“When I open the bottle, the minute will try to rejoin time. The watch may anchor it. If it does, we’ll see what happened at nine eleven.”

“And if it doesn’t?”

“Run.”

“Upstairs?”

“Preferably into tomorrow.”

Before Mara could ask what that meant, Elias broke the seal.

Grey mist burst from the bottle.

The mirrors went dark.

The broken watch began to tick.

Around them, the Archive disappeared.

Fog covered everything.

Elias stood in the middle of the northern bridge. Mara was beside him, though she appeared pale and transparent. Bells rang somewhere beyond the whiteness.

A man hurried toward them.

He wore house slippers.

“Father!” Mara cried.

The man passed through her.

Jon Venn looked over his shoulder, terrified. In his hand he carried a roll of blueprints. Behind him, something moved in the fog.

Not a person.

A shadow stretched across the bridge, thin as the hand of a clock. It swept over the stones in a slow arc. Wherever it passed, frost appeared.

Jon ran.

At the center of the bridge, he stopped and tore open the blueprints. Elias recognized diagrams of the city’s clock towers, connected by lines that converged beneath the western tower.

Jon stared directly toward Elias.

“You,” he said.

Elias stepped back, though he knew this was only a recovered moment.

Jon pulled a brass key from his pocket and pushed it into a crack between two stones.

The shadow reached him.

For an instant, the fog turned black.

Jon vanished.

The world snapped apart.

Elias found himself on the Archive floor. The mirrors had shattered. Mara knelt beside the broken watch, calling for her father.

The minute was gone.

But on the table lay a roll of blueprints.

Mara seized them.

“He left these in the memory.”

“No,” Elias said quietly. “Memories cannot leave objects.”

“Then where did they come from?”

He had no answer.

They spread the plans across the floor. Jon had mapped the city’s network of clocks and underground pipes. Red ink marked a chamber beyond the Archive, though Elias knew of no such room.

Across the drawing, Jon had written:

THE CLOCKS ARE NOT COLLECTING LOST TIME.

THEY ARE CAUSING IT.

Mara read the sentence twice.

Elias sat down heavily.

For thirty-eight years, he had believed the Archive protected the city. The clocks gathered forgotten moments before they could decay and damage the present. That was what the former Keeper had taught him.

But the former Keeper had also taught him never to ask why.

They searched the Archive walls until midnight.

Behind the furnace, Mara found a keyhole hidden beneath soot.

“The key from the bridge,” she said.

They waited for low tide, then descended to the river. Between the stones where Jon had pushed it, they found the brass key.

It opened a door behind the furnace.

Beyond it, stairs spiraled downward.

The air grew colder as Elias and Mara descended. The ticking above faded, replaced by a deeper rhythm.

A heartbeat.

At the bottom lay a cavern large enough to hold a cathedral. Pipes descended from every direction, joining a vast machine of iron gears. At its center hung a pendulum shaped like a black blade.

With each swing, blue sparks rose from the machinery and vanished into the pipes.

Mara whispered, “What is it?”

“The master clock.”

“No,” said a voice behind them. “It is a mouth.”

A man stepped from the shadows.

He was thin, bearded, and barefoot. His clothes hung in tatters.

“Father?”

Jon Venn smiled.

Mara ran to him.

Elias turned away as they embraced. He watched the black pendulum sweep across the cavern.

Jon had survived for nearly a year inside the hidden chamber. The machine, he explained, did not merely store lost time. It consumed it. The clocks stole tiny pieces from the people of Bellwether and fed those pieces into something beneath the city.

“What?” Elias asked.

Jon pointed downward.

“The future.”

The master clock powered Bellwether’s prosperity by borrowing time from lives not yet lived. Every avoided accident, every profitable coincidence, every storm that turned aside at the city walls was purchased with minutes stolen from its citizens.

“At first, it took moments no one noticed,” Jon said. “Waiting. Sleeping. Forgetting. But it became hungry. During the fog, it took seven people.”

“Why weren’t you consumed?” Mara asked.

“I had the key. I fell through the maintenance door before the shadow reached me. The others weren’t so fortunate.”

Mara gripped his hand.

“Can we stop it?”

Jon looked at Elias.

“The Keeper can.”

Elias gazed at the machine. “How?”

“The Archive holds more than a million hours. Return them all at once. Flood the system. The master clock will break.”

“And the city?”

“All the borrowed fortune will end.”

“What does that mean?”

“Storms may strike. Accidents may happen. Businesses may fail. People will face all the ordinary dangers the clock kept away.”

Elias thought of the crowded streets, the ferries, the hospitals, the children.

“How many will die?”

Jon’s silence was answer enough.

Mara stepped between them. “How many will die if we do nothing?”

“Eventually?” Jon said. “Everyone. The clock will take years, then lives, then generations.”

Above them, the city began to chime one in the morning.

The master pendulum swung.

Elias saw the blue bottle in his mind.

His lost hour.

Clara’s voice.

All his life, he had imagined that the worst thing time could do was take something away. Now he understood that time was not cruel because it passed. It was cruel only when someone tried to own it.

“I’ll open the Archive,” he said.

They climbed back before dawn.

The release mechanism stood beside the receiving tank: a wheel Elias had polished every week but never turned. It would open every bottle simultaneously and send the contents upward through the clocks.

Jon went to warn the hospitals and ferry captains. Mara remained with Elias.

“You should go with your father,” he told her.

“I’ve spent a year looking for him. I can spare ten minutes.”

“There may not be ten minutes.”

“Then you shouldn’t waste them arguing.”

Together they unlocked the shelves.

Thousands of bottles began to glow. Gold, silver, red, green, and grey light filled the underground hall until it seemed they stood inside a jewel.

Elias held the blue bottle.

“You’re going to open yours first,” Mara said.

“No.”

“You want to.”

“That’s why I mustn’t.”

“What if it tells you something important?”

“What if it tells me something I can’t bear?”

Mara considered this.

“My mother says unbearable things are usually borne because there isn’t a choice.”

“Your mother sounds exhausting too.”

“She is.”

The first light of dawn touched the high windows.

The city clocks stirred.

Elias broke the blue bottle.

The lost hour opened around him.

He stood in a garden forty years younger.

White roses grew beside a stone wall. Clara waited beneath an apple tree, wearing a blue ribbon in her hair.

Young Elias entered through the gate.

“You came,” Clara said.

“You asked me to.”

“I need to tell you why I can’t marry you.”

The older Elias moved closer, his heart aching with the ancient freshness of the scene.

Clara took the young man’s hands.

“I’m ill,” she said. “The doctor says I may have a year. Perhaps less.”

Young Elias stared at her.

“Then we’ll have a year.”

“I won’t make you watch me die.”

“You don’t get to choose what I can endure.”

“I’ve already chosen.”

They argued. They wept. Clara begged him to forget her.

Then the courthouse clock struck six.

A shadow passed across the garden.

The young Elias blinked.

Clara stepped back, confusion crossing her face. The last hour vanished from both of them, stolen cleanly away. What remained was only the ending: Clara refusing him, Elias wounded and bewildered.

The lost hour trembled.

For the first time, the older Elias saw beyond it, into the days that followed. Clara had not left the city. She had entered Saint Orra’s Hospital under her mother’s name.

She died eleven months later.

Elias had walked past her window every week without knowing.

The vision faded.

He stood again in the Archive, tears on his face.

Mara touched his sleeve. “I’m sorry.”

“I had a year,” he whispered. “It stole a year from us.”

“No,” Mara said. “It stole an hour. The rest was stolen by what you believed afterward.”

The truth of it struck more deeply than comfort.

Elias looked at the shelves. All those bottles. All those moments around which people had built mistaken lives.

He took hold of the release wheel.

Mara gripped it beside him.

They turned.

At first, nothing happened.

Then the Archive sang.

Bottles shattered in waves. A million lost hours rose as light, filling the hall, spiraling up the tower, racing through the pipes beneath Bellwether.

Across the city, clocks spun backward.

People stopped in the streets as forgotten moments returned.

A baker remembered his mother’s final words. A widow recovered the sound of her husband laughing. A soldier recalled the face of the man who had spared him. Children woke from dreams they had lost years before.

The master clock screamed beneath the earth.

The floor buckled.

“Run!” Elias shouted.

They raced up the stairs as shelves collapsed behind them. Light burst through the brass door. Outside, every bell in Bellwether rang at once.

The western tower split from top to bottom.

Elias and Mara reached the square as the great clock face exploded into golden dust.

Then came silence.

True silence.

For the first time in centuries, no clock ticked anywhere in Bellwether.

The sun rose.

It was not a fortunate day.

A ferry struck a sandbar. Rain flooded the lower market. A chimney collapsed on Weaver Street, though no one was killed. The price of wheat fell, three engagements ended, and the mayor discovered that most of his investments were worthless.

Yet people also found the seven citizens lost during the Long Fog. They emerged from doorways, cellars, and forgotten alleys, exactly as they had been, carrying no memory of the missing year.

Jon Venn went home in slippers.

The western tower was never rebuilt.

In its place, the city made a garden. White roses grew beside a low stone wall, and in the center stood a simple sundial with no numbers.

Elias retired as Keeper because there was nothing left to keep. He opened a small repair shop on River Street, next to the candle seller. He repaired watches, though he refused to guarantee their accuracy.

Mara visited every afternoon after school. She became his apprentice, then his partner, and eventually a better clockmaker than he had ever been.

Years later, when Elias was old and often forgot where he had placed his spectacles, Mara found him sitting in the garden beneath the ruined tower.

“Do you know what time it is?” she asked.

He looked at the unmarked sundial.

“No.”

“Neither do I.”

“Good.”

Children played in the square. Ferries sounded on the river. Somewhere, a woman sang from an open window.

Elias closed his eyes.

For most of his life, he had believed an hour was a vessel: something that could be filled, stored, stolen, or returned. Now he knew better.

An hour was not a possession.

It was a door.

All anyone could do was walk through before it closed.

Mara sat beside him, and together they listened as the city moved forward without counting.
